title: Quantum Data Tasks
intro: When the inputs are themselves quantum states, a reservoir can process them without a classical encoding step: the state is fed into the reservoir, measured, and a trained readout estimates its properties. Linear properties (expectation values, tomography) are learned exactly by a linear readout of an informationally complete reservoir; nonlinear ones (purity, entanglement) need nonlinear readouts or several copies.

blocks.text: What you need first

The effective-POVM view of Quantum Extreme Learning Machines (#/qrc/models/quantum-extreme-learning-machines) (this page continues it directly), density matrices and entanglement from Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) and Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement), and the measurement postulate from Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement). Ridge regression: Linear Regression and the Ridge Readout (#/qrc/start/linear-regression-and-ridge).
What you will be able to do

items: Describe how a reservoir can be used to estimate properties of an unknown quantum state without a calibrated measurement, and what is trained.
Say which properties a linear readout of single-copy statistics can and cannot learn, and prove the impossibility for purity.
Use two copies and the swap trick to turn a nonlinear property (purity, pure-state entanglement) into a linear one, and compute it for an example state.
Explain the bias of products of finite-shot estimates and how to avoid it.
List what a quantum-data reservoir saves and what it does not (tomography cost, labelled training states).

blocks.text: When the input is a quantum state
Why we need it

Suppose an experiment produces an unknown two-qubit state, over and over, and you want to know one thing about it: is it entangled? What is its purity? What is the expectation value of some observable? The textbook route is quantum state tomography: measure in many bases, then reconstruct. That needs a well-characterised measurement apparatus and a model of it. In a real laboratory the apparatus is imperfect, and its imperfections drift. A quantum reservoir offers another route: let the unknown state enter a fixed, messy, but stable system, measure it in one simple fixed way, and learn what the statistics mean by training on states whose properties you already know.
The idea in plain words

Think of a bathroom scale that is not calibrated. You do not need to open it and measure its springs. Put on a few weights you know, note what it reads, and fit a line. After that, any reading translates into a weight. The reservoir is the uncalibrated scale; the labelled states are the known weights; the linear readout is the fitted line. The picture breaks in one way: a scale measures one number, whereas a quantum state has many properties, and you have to decide which function of the state you are fitting, because (as we will see) some functions are not linear in the state.
Quantum reservoir processing

Ghosh, Opala, Matuszewski, Paterek and Liew proposed quantum reservoir processing: input quantum states (two optical modes) are coupled, one mode after the other through a cascaded scheme, into a fixed, disordered lattice of coupled, incoherently pumped fermionic sites; the site occupations are measured, and a linear readout trained on known states estimates a property of new ones. They demonstrated, in simulation, qualitative tasks such as recognising entangled states and quantitative ones such as estimating nonlinear functions of the input state (entropy, purity, logarithmic negativity); a follow-up paper used the same kind of network for full state reconstruction. Their readout is linear and each input passes through once. This does not contradict the argument below that no single-copy linear readout equals the purity on all states: their estimators are trained and tested on restricted families of input states (for example squeezed thermal states), on which a linear functional of $\rho$ can track a nonlinear property closely. The advantage over textbook tomography is practical: the reservoir is not engineered to implement a particular measurement basis; any fixed, generic, rich enough dynamics will do, and the calibration is replaced by training.
The measurement as an effective POVM
The maths, step by step

An input state $\rho$ on $d$ dimensions joins a reservoir of $m$ qubits in $\vert0\rangle$, a fixed unitary $U$ acts on the whole register, and the register is measured in the computational basis. The outcome probabilities are

blocks.caption: Effective POVM element on the input from outcome k.

items: Step 1. The joint state before the unitary is $\rho\otimes\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$.
Step 2. After $U$ and projecting on outcome $k$: $p_k=\langle k\vert U(\rho\otimes\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert)U^\dagger\vert k\rangle$.

Step 3. Define $A_k$ as the operator from the input space to the outcome-$k$ amplitude, $A_k=\langle k\vert U\vert\cdot,\,0\rangle$, a $1\times d$ row vector for each fixed ancilla part. Then $p_k=A_k\rho A_k^\dagger=\operatorname{Tr}[A_k^\dagger A_k\rho]$.
Step 4. So $E_k=A_k^\dagger A_k$: positive, and $\sum_kE_k=I$ because $U$ is unitary.

blocks.text: The readout $\sum_kw_kp_k$ is then the expectation of $O_w=\sum_kw_kE_k$. If $\{E_k\}$ spans all $d\times d$ operators (rank $d^2$), any observable is reachable, and training finds the weights that represent it. That is tomography by regression: train on states with known expectation values, and the readout learns the inverse of the measurement map without anyone writing that map down.
A worked example: why the unitary matters

Let the input be one qubit and the reservoir one ancilla in $\vert0\rangle$, and suppose $U$ is a CNOT with the input as control. For an input basis state $\vert x\rangle$ the output is $\vert x,x\rangle$. So outcome $k=(a,b)$ has amplitude $\langle a b\vert x,x\rangle=\delta_{ax}\delta_{bx}$: $A_{00}=\langle0\vert$, $A_{11}=\langle1\vert$, $A_{01}=A_{10}=0$. Then $E_{00}=\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$, $E_{11}=\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert$ and the others vanish. The span is $\{\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert,\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert\}$: dimension 2 of the 4 needed. This reservoir can learn functions of $\langle Z\rangle$ and nothing about the coherences. Replacing $U$ by something that rotates the input before the CNOT adds other operators to the span; the program below finds the rank for random $U$.
Linear versus nonlinear targets
Why we need it
Tomography by regression sounds like it can learn any property. It cannot, and the reason is simple enough to prove on the back of an envelope.
The maths

A linear readout of single-copy statistics can only produce functions of the form $\operatorname{Tr}[O\rho]$. Many interesting properties are not of that form. The purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$ is quadratic in $\rho$; entanglement measures (concurrence, negativity, entanglement entropy) are nonlinear. A clean argument for purity:

items: Step 1. $\rho_1=\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$ and $\rho_2=\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert$ both have purity 1.
Step 2. Suppose a linear function $f(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}[O\rho]$ equals the purity on both: $f(\rho_1)=f(\rho_2)=1$.
Step 3. Linearity gives $f(\tfrac12\rho_1+\tfrac12\rho_2)=\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot1=1$.
Step 4. But $\tfrac12(\rho_1+\rho_2)=I/2$ has purity $\operatorname{Tr}(I/2)^2=\tfrac12$. Contradiction.

blocks.text: There are three ways around it: a nonlinear readout (products of probabilities, which estimates $\operatorname{Tr}[(O\otimes O')(\rho\otimes\rho)]$ when the products come from independent copies), feeding two copies of the state into the reservoir at once (then $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathrm{SWAP}\,\rho\otimes\rho]$ is linear in $\rho\otimes\rho$), or a reservoir whose dynamics itself depends nonlinearly on the input (not possible for a fixed channel acting on one copy: channels are linear).
A simulation

The program makes this concrete. Inputs are random 2-qubit states (a random pure state mixed with $I/4$ by a random weight). The reservoir has $m$ extra qubits in $\vert0\rangle$ and a Haar-random unitary on all $2+m$ qubits; the features are the $2^{2+m}$ exact outcome probabilities. Two targets: $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$ (linear) and the purity (quadratic). Two readouts: linear in the probabilities, and quadratic (all products $p_ip_j$ as well). Then $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$ is estimated from $S$ shots per state.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
I2 = np.eye(2); X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1])
def haar(d):
    z = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(d, d))) / np.sqrt(2)
    q, r = np.linalg.qr(z); return q * (np.diag(r) / abs(np.diag(r)))
def random_input():                       # a 2-qubit state, pure or partly mixed
    v = rng.normal(size=4) + 1j * rng.normal(size=4); v /= np.linalg.norm(v)
    p = rng.uniform(0, 1)
    return p * np.outer(v, v.conj()) + (1 - p) * np.eye(4) / 4
def povm(m, U):
    """Effective POVM on the 2 input qubits: reservoir of m qubits in |0..0>, unitary U, Z-basis readout of all."""
    anc = np.zeros(2 ** m); anc[0] = 1
    E = []
    for k in range(2 ** (2 + m)):
        row = U[k].reshape(4, 2 ** m) @ anc        # <k| U (. (x) |0..0>)
        E.append(np.outer(row.conj(), row))         # E_k = A_k^dagger A_k
    return E
def probs(E, rho): return np.array([np.real(np.trace(e @ rho)) for e in E])
paulis = [np.kron(a, b) for a in (I2, X, Y, Z) for b in (I2, X, Y, Z)]
train = [random_input() for _ in range(400)]; test = [random_input() for _ in range(200)]
targets = {"<X(x)X>": lambda r: np.real(np.trace(r @ np.kron(X, X))),
           "purity Tr rho^2": lambda r: np.real(np.trace(r @ r))}
def fit(Ftr, ytr, Fte, yte):
    A = lambda F: np.hstack([F, np.ones((len(F), 1))])
    w = np.linalg.lstsq(A(Ftr), ytr, rcond=1e-10)[0]
    return np.mean((A(Fte) @ w - yte) ** 2) / np.var(yte)
quad = lambda P: np.hstack([P, np.einsum("ti,tj->tij", P, P).reshape(len(P), -1)])
for m in (1, 2, 3):
    E = povm(m, haar(2 ** (2 + m)))
    rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.array([[np.real(np.trace(e @ p)) for p in paulis] for e in E]), 1e-9)
    Ptr = np.array([probs(E, r) for r in train]); Pte = np.array([probs(E, r) for r in test])
    out = [f"m={m} reservoir qubits: {2 ** (2 + m)} outcomes, POVM rank {rank} of 16"]
    for name, f in targets.items():
        ytr = np.array([f(r) for r in train]); yte = np.array([f(r) for r in test])
        out.append(f"{name}: linear NMSE {fit(Ptr, ytr, Pte, yte):.3f}, quadratic NMSE {fit(quad(Ptr), ytr, quad(Pte), yte):.3f}")
    print("; ".join(out))
# shot noise: estimate <X(x)X> from S shots per input state with m = 3
E = povm(3, haar(32)); ytr = np.array([targets["<X(x)X>"](r) for r in train]); yte = np.array([targets["<X(x)X>"](r) for r in test])
Ptr = np.array([probs(E, r) for r in train]); Pte = np.array([probs(E, r) for r in test])
for S in (100, 1000, 10000):
    sample = lambda P: np.array([rng.multinomial(S, np.clip(p, 0, None) / np.clip(p, 0, None).sum()) / S for p in P])
    print(f"<X(x)X> from {S} shots per state: NMSE {fit(sample(Ptr), ytr, sample(Pte), yte):.3f}")

items: $m=1$: 8 outcomes, POVM rank 8 of the 16 needed. $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$: linear NMSE $0.480$, quadratic $0.446$. Purity: linear $0.978$, quadratic $0.249$. Not IC, so neither target is fully reachable.
$m=2$: 16 outcomes, rank 16: IC. $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$ linear NMSE $0.000$; purity linear $0.986$ (impossible, as argued) and quadratic $0.000$.
$m=3$: 32 outcomes, rank still 16 (it cannot exceed $d^2$); the same scores.
Shots, $m=3$: $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$ NMSE $0.552$ at 100 shots per state, $0.160$ at 1000, $0.023$ at 10000.

blocks.text: Two remarks on the quadratic readout. It works here because the probabilities are exact. With shot noise, products $\hat p_i\hat p_j$ from the same shots are biased estimates of $p_ip_j$. For multinomial counts, $\operatorname{Var}(\hat p_i)=p_i(1-p_i)/S$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat p_i,\hat p_j)=-p_ip_j/S$, so $\mathbb{E}[\hat p_i^2]=p_i^2+p_i(1-p_i)/S$ and $\mathbb{E}[\hat p_i\hat p_j]=p_ip_j(1-1/S)$ for $i\ne j$. For $p_i=0.3$ and $S=100$ the squared estimate is too large by $0.3\times0.7/100=0.0021$ on average: small, but the same order as the structure the readout is trying to learn. Either correct the bias or form products from disjoint batches of shots, which is the same as using two copies. And the 136 distinct products of 16 probabilities need many more training states than the 16 linear features (152 features against 400 training states in the sample).

blocks.title: Check yourself: purity is not linear
blocks.text: A linear readout is trained to output the purity and gets it right on $\rho_1=\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$ and $\rho_2=\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert$. What does it output on $\rho=\tfrac12(\rho_1+\rho_2)$, and what is the true value?
blocks.hint: Use linearity on the equal mixture.
solution: So no linear readout of single-copy statistics represents purity; in the sample the best linear fit leaves NMSE $0.986$.
blocks.answer: It outputs 1; the true purity is 1/2

blocks.text: Entanglement from a reservoir
The maths

For pure two-qubit states entanglement is a quadratic function of the state: with $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B\vert\psi\rangle\langle\psi\vert$, the concurrence satisfies $C^2=2(1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2)$, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=\operatorname{Tr}[(\mathrm{SWAP}_A\otimes I_B)\,\rho\otimes\rho]$ is linear in two copies. (Here $\mathrm{SWAP}_A$ exchanges the $A$ halves of the two copies; I checked the identity numerically on a random pure state: both sides gave $0.8074$.) So the same quadratic readout that learns purity learns pure-state entanglement. For mixed states, measures like the negativity involve eigenvalues of the partial transpose and are not polynomials of fixed degree; a reservoir with a polynomial readout approximates them, and an entanglement witness (a linear $\operatorname{Tr}[W\rho]<0$ test) is learnable exactly by a linear readout of an IC reservoir, but only one witness at a time.
A worked example
Take $\vert\psi\rangle=\cos\theta\vert00\rangle+\sin\theta\vert11\rangle$ with $\theta=\pi/8$.

items: Step 1. $\rho_A=\operatorname{diag}(\cos^2\theta,\sin^2\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(0.854,0.146)$.
Step 2. $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2=\cos^4\theta+\sin^4\theta=0.729+0.021=0.75$ (using $\cos^4+\sin^4=1-\tfrac12\sin^22\theta=1-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12$).
Step 3. Concurrence $C=2\vert ad-bc\vert=2\cos\theta\sin\theta=\sin2\theta=\sin(\pi/4)=0.7071$.

blocks.title: Check yourself: concurrence from reduced purity
blocks.text: For $\theta=\pi/4$ (a Bell state) give $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2$ and the concurrence.
Quantum inputs over time

With memory, a reservoir can be fed a stream of quantum states and asked about past ones. Tran and Nakajima formulated temporal quantum tomography: a stream of input states interacts repeatedly with a quantum reservoir, and a linear readout of the reservoir's measurement data is trained to learn relations between quantum channels applied to the input stream, such as recovering a state injected several steps earlier. They also proposed a quantum short-term memory capacity to quantify this ability; reconstruction of older inputs degrades as the reservoir's memory fades, as the linear memory function does for classical inputs (see Memory and Processing Capacity (#/qrc/foundations/memory-and-capacity)). Related tasks: predicting the output state of an unknown quantum channel from its inputs, and estimating properties of a quantum process over time.
Where it helps and where it does not

items: It helps when the measurement apparatus is uncharacterised or drifting: the reservoir plus training absorbs the unknown POVM, so no model of the device is needed, only labelled training states.

It does not reduce the sample complexity of tomography: estimating all $d^2-1$ parameters still needs a number of copies growing at least linearly with $d^2$, and the conditioning of a random POVM is worse than that of a designed one (the factor $2292$ against $3$ on Quantum Extreme Learning Machines (#/qrc/models/quantum-extreme-learning-machines)). For predicting a few observables, randomised measurement schemes (classical shadows) have provable guarantees with sample counts set by the observables, not by $d$.
Training needs labelled quantum states: states whose properties you already know, prepared reliably. Preparing that training set is often the hardest part of an experiment.
Single-copy linear readouts can never estimate nonlinear properties without bias; design for two copies, or accept the bias of products of finite-shot estimates.

blocks.text: Common mistake: reading the quadratic-readout success in the sample as proof that a one-copy reservoir computes purity. It does with exact probabilities (NMSE $0.000$) because the table has no shot noise; with finite shots the products are biased as computed above, and two honest copies are the clean way.
Putting it together

Problem. An experiment makes unknown 2-qubit pure states and you want their concurrence. You have a reservoir with $m=2$ ancillas (a 4-qubit register, 16 outcomes) and you can run $10^4$ shots per state. Design the estimator and say what training set you need.

items: Step 1. For pure states $C=\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2)}$, so the target to learn is the purity of one half, a quadratic function of $\rho$. A linear one-copy readout cannot do it (the impossibility proof above).

Step 2. Option A: quadratic readout of one copy: $16+16\cdot17/2=152$ features. Needs several hundred labelled training states and unbiased product estimates (disjoint shot batches). Option B: two copies at once, 4 input qubits ($d=16$), IC would need $256$ effects, but we need only one operator, $\mathrm{SWAP}_A$, which a linear readout of a rich enough reservoir can represent with far fewer; I did not test this option here.

Step 3. Training set. Labelled pure states with known concurrence, e.g. the family $\cos\theta\vert00\rangle+\sin\theta\vert11\rangle$ and its local rotations (a generic pure state is related to this family by local unitaries). Preparing these reliably is the hard part.
Step 4. Check: predict the concurrence of a Bell state (1) and of $\theta=\pi/8$ (0.7071) as a calibration test; deviations beyond the shot-noise error show a bias.

blocks.text: The skeleton of the answer is general: decide whether the target is linear in the state, fix it with copies or a quadratic readout, count the features and the training states, and test on cases you can compute by hand.
Key points

items: A reservoir with a fixed measurement is an effective POVM $E_k=A_k^\dagger A_k$ on the unknown state; the readout computes $\operatorname{Tr}[O_w\rho]$.
If the POVM is informationally complete (rank $d^2$) every linear property is learnable by training on labelled states, with no model of the apparatus.
Nonlinear properties (purity, entanglement) are not learnable by a single-copy linear readout: the equal mixture of two pure basis states gives the contradiction.
Two copies and the swap trick make purity linear: $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathrm{SWAP}\,\rho\otimes\rho]$; for pure two-qubit states $C^2=2(1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2)$.
Products of finite-shot estimates are biased: $\mathbb{E}[\hat p_i^2]=p_i^2+p_i(1-p_i)/S$.
The gains are calibration-free measurement and robustness to drift; the costs are labelled training states and tomography's unavoidable scaling.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Purity is not linear
blocks.text: A linear readout is trained to output the purity and gets it right on $\rho_1=\vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$ and $\rho_2=\vert1\rangle\langle1\vert$. What does it output on $\rho=\tfrac12(\rho_1+\rho_2)$, and what is the true value?
solution: So no linear readout of single-copy statistics represents purity; in the sample the best linear fit leaves NMSE $0.986$.
blocks.answer: It outputs 1; the true purity is 1/2

blocks.title: Concurrence from reduced purity
blocks.text: For $\vert\psi\rangle=\cos\theta\vert00\rangle+\sin\theta\vert11\rangle$ with $\theta=\pi/8$, compute $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2$ and the concurrence, and check $C^2=2(1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2)$.

blocks.title: Shots for one expectation value
blocks.text: You estimate $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$, whose true value is near 0, by measuring it directly (outcomes $\pm1$). How many shots give a standard error of $0.01$? Why does the reservoir estimate in the sample, at $10^4$ shots, still leave NMSE $0.023$?
solution: Variance per shot $1-\langle XX\rangle^2\approx1$, so the standard error is $1/\sqrt S$ and $S=10^4$.

The reservoir spreads the information over 32 outcome probabilities and the readout reconstructs $\langle XX\rangle$ as a weighted sum; the weights amplify the shot noise of each $\hat p_k$, and the readout was also trained on noisy features, which biases it.
A designed measurement of $X\otimes X$ is the best case for one observable; the reservoir's strength is learning many observables from the same data without a model of the device.
blocks.answer: $10^4$ shots; the readout weights amplify the noise in each probability

blocks.title: Bias of a product
blocks.text: Two outcome frequencies from $S=50$ shots estimate probabilities $p_1=0.2$ and $p_2=0.5$. What are the expected values of $\hat p_1\hat p_2$ and of $\hat p_1^2$ in terms of the true values, and by how much do they differ from $p_1p_2$ and $p_1^2$?
solution: The square is biased up, the cross product down; both biases shrink as $1/S$. Using disjoint shot batches for the two factors removes both.

blocks.text: Where this is used

The same effective-POVM and noise-amplification analysis is in Quantum Extreme Learning Machines (#/qrc/models/quantum-extreme-learning-machines); the cost of shots per input is the subject of Resource Accounting (#/qrc/hardware/resource-accounting), and how well a generic reservoir can represent such maps in principle is in Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality). With a stream of quantum inputs and memory the framework joins the time-series material of The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir).
